title: Dictionary
description: Key terms and concepts in context engineering, token economics, and AI-assisted development.

terms.definition: The maximum number of tokens (input + output) a model can process in a single request. Think of it as the AI’s short-term memory or desk: everything must fit on the desk at once. Current models range from 200K tokens (Claude Haiku 4.5) to 1.05M tokens (GPT-5.5).

The discipline of designing and managing the information provided to an AI model to maximize output quality while minimizing token costs. Encompasses prompt design, file selection, caching strategy, and context window management.

Instead of loading an entire codebase, which would immediately overwhelm the attention budget, modern agents use JIT (just-in-time) context. The assistant dynamically loads only the necessary data at runtime, revealing information progressively as needed.

The assistant maintains references (file paths, stored queries) and dynamically loads only the necessary data at runtime using tools like grep, head, or tail. This avoids stuffing the full content into the context window upfront.

When a session nears its token limit, the assistant summarizes critical details, such as architectural decisions and unresolved bugs, while discarding redundant tool outputs. This reclaims context budget without losing essential information.

A lighter form of compaction where the raw results of previous tool calls (like long terminal outputs or file reads) are cleared to save space, while keeping the conclusions and decisions derived from them.

The agent maintains an external NOTES.md or to-do list to track dependencies and progress across thousands of steps. After a context reset, it can read these notes back to restore essential state without replaying the full history.

Files or code snippets that are topically related to the query but do not contain the answer. These can cause the model to lose focus or hallucinate, degrading output quality. Effective context engineering actively filters distractors.

As more tokens are added to a conversation, the model’s ability to accurately retrieve specific pieces of information from the context decreases. Long conversations suffer from degraded attention, making early details harder to recall.

The accumulation of irrelevant, redundant, or misleading information in the context window that degrades model performance. Includes distractors, context rot, and poor structural patterns. Fighting context pollution is a core challenge of context engineering.

A simple context management strategy that keeps only the last N conversation turns and discards older ones. Fast and predictable but loses early context completely. Best for simple chatbots where recent context matters most.

A context management strategy that condenses the full conversation history into a compact executive summary before each new turn. Preserves the big picture but loses verbatim detail and adds latency from the summarisation LLM call.

An API-level context management feature that clears old content by rule before the request reaches the model; no secondary model reviews the conversation. clear_tool_uses_20250919 removes old tool results once input passes a trigger (default 100K tokens), keeps the most recent 3 tool uses by default, and supports clear_at_least, exclude_tools, and clear_tool_inputs; clear_thinking_20251015 removes earlier thinking blocks. Both use the beta header context-management-2025-06-27.

An external persistent storage mechanism (like a filing cabinet) that the model can read from and write to across sessions. Unlike the context window (short-term desk), the memory tool persists information permanently. Used for user preferences, project knowledge, and cross-session continuity.

An API feature that summarizes earlier conversation history inside the request pipeline. Anthropic's server-side compaction runs in threshold mode (compact_20260112, beta compact-2026-01-12) when input tokens pass a trigger, or on demand (compaction: {type: "summarize"}, beta compact-2026-09-04) when the application asks. It replaces the SDK compaction_control helper, which is deprecated in the TypeScript and Ruby SDKs and removed in Python SDK v1.0.

The input-token count at which server-side compaction runs, set with the trigger field in the API (for example {"type": "input_tokens", "value": 150000}). The default is 150K input tokens and the minimum is 50K. context_token_threshold was the name of this setting in the deprecated SDK compaction_control helper.

The fundamental unit of text processing for LLMs. A token is roughly 3-4 characters or 0.75 words in English. All API pricing is based on token counts. Understanding tokenization is essential for cost estimation.

Tokens sent to the model in a request, including system prompts, conversation history, and user messages. Input tokens are typically cheaper than output tokens and form the bulk of context window usage.

Tokens generated by the model in response. Output tokens typically cost 5-8x more than input tokens (5x on current Claude models). Controlling output length through instructions and max_tokens is a key cost optimization lever.

The objective of context engineering: provide the smallest possible set of tokens that maximize the likelihood of correct code generation. Every token should contribute meaningfully to the model’s understanding.
Standard pricing unit for LLM APIs. For example, Claude Sonnet 5.5 costs $2/MTok input and $10/MTok output, with cache reads at $0.10/MTok. This metric allows comparison across providers and models.

A pricing tier where prompts above a token threshold are billed at higher rates for the whole request, not just the tokens past the threshold. Claude Haiku 5.5 switches above 100K input tokens, most OpenAI models from GPT-5.4 onward above 272K, and Gemini 3.1 Pro above 200K. Budget estimates for large contexts must account for the jump.

The complete set of instructions and context sent to an AI model in a single request. Includes system instructions, user message, conversation history, and any retrieved context. The quality of the prompt directly determines the quality of the output.

A technique where frequently-used prompt prefixes are stored server-side, allowing subsequent requests with the same prefix to be processed at reduced cost. Cache reads cost 90% or more below base input on current models. Requires a minimum token threshold to activate.

The cost of storing a prompt prefix in the cache for the first time. On Claude, 5-minute cache writes cost 1.25x base input (Claude Sonnet 5.5: $2.50/MTok vs. $2/MTok) and 1-hour cache writes cost 2x base input. The write pays for itself once the same prefix is read back.

The cost of using a previously cached prompt prefix. Cache reads cost 0.1x base input on most Claude models, 0.05x on Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 (Sonnet 5.5: $0.10/MTok vs. $2/MTok), and 0.025x on Claude Fable 5.1. The break-even point depends on how many times the cached prefix is reused.
The number of requests after which prompt caching becomes cost-effective compared to standard pricing. Calculated from cache write cost vs. cumulative savings from cache reads.

Instructions provided at the beginning of a conversation to set the model’s behavior, personality, and constraints. System prompts are ideal candidates for caching since they remain constant across requests.

Using tags like <background_information>, <tool_guidance>, <constraints> to clearly separate different types of instructions in prompts. This structural technique helps models parse complex multi-section prompts more reliably.
A prompting technique where the model is instructed to show its reasoning step by step before giving a final answer. Improves accuracy on complex tasks but increases output token usage.

A model capability where additional compute is used for internal reasoning before generating a response. Fixed thinking budgets (budget_tokens) return a 400 error on Claude Opus 4.7 and later and on 5.x models; adaptive thinking, steered by effort and task budgets, replaces them.

An API setting (output_config.effort) that controls how thoroughly a model works on a request. The levels low, medium, high, xhigh, and max trade thoroughness for tokens. The default is high, except medium on Claude Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5.

A pattern where relevant documents are retrieved from a knowledge base and injected into the context before generation. Enables models to reference up-to-date or domain-specific information without fine-tuning.

Research finding that models often perform differently on shuffled vs. logically structured context. The placement and organization of information within the context window affects retrieval accuracy and generation quality.

An economic production function adapted for AI cost analysis. Models the relationship between token inputs (quantity and quality) and output quality, helping find the optimal trade-off between cost and performance.
A technique used in IDE extensions to rank open editor tabs by their relevance to the current task. Factors include import relationships, path similarity, edit recency, and diagnostic overlap.

The effective amount of context a model can meaningfully attend to. While context windows may be large (200K to 1M+ tokens), attention quality degrades with length. The practical attention budget is often smaller than the raw token limit.

A real-time visualization showing current token usage across the context window, broken down by category (system prompt, conversation history, file contents, tool outputs). Helps developers stay within limits.

A Tokalator dashboard estimate built from logged turns: the average input tokens per turn, the projected size of the next turn, and how many turns remain before the context window fills. It is an input-only estimate, since output tokens and cache hits are not observable from the editor.
An API tier that processes requests asynchronously at reduced cost, ideal for non-time-sensitive workloads like bulk analysis or testing. Typically offers the lowest per-token pricing.

The ability of a model to invoke external functions or tools during generation. The model outputs structured parameters that the client executes, returning results back into the context. Enables agentic workflows.

A strategy where context is loaded dynamically at runtime rather than pre-loaded. The IDE or agent fetches only the files, symbols, or data needed for the current step, similar to how modern IDEs lazy-load imports. Reduces waste and keeps the context window focused.

Custom instructions that control how compaction summarizes conversation history. In Anthropic's server-side compaction this is the instructions parameter, which replaces the default summarization prompt rather than adding to it, so it must ask for everything the task needs kept (for example order IDs, account numbers, and resolution status).

Reusable packages of domain expertise defined in SKILL.md files that provide specialized capabilities, knowledge, and refined workflows to AI agents. Skills can be scoped to specific domains like testing strategies, API design, or performance optimization, and can be invoked as slash commands or loaded automatically by the model.

Deterministic shell commands that run at key lifecycle points during agent sessions. Claude Code's hooks reference lists over 30 events, including PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, PermissionRequest, UserPromptSubmit, Stop, SubagentStart, SubagentStop, PreCompact, PostCompact, SessionStart, and SessionEnd. Unlike instructions that guide behavior, hooks execute code with guaranteed outcomes, which is useful for enforcing security policies, automating code quality checks, or creating audit trails.

An agent interaction pattern where a follow-up message signals the currently running request to yield after finishing the active tool execution, then processes the new message immediately. Used to redirect an agent heading in the wrong direction without cancelling or waiting for the full response to complete.

A GitHub Copilot feature, in public preview, that lets Copilot store facts it learns about a repository and the user's preferences, then use them in later tasks. Memories that go unused for 28 days are deleted automatically.

A pattern where multiple specialized subagents collaborate to achieve a complex goal, each operating in its own dedicated context window. Enables context efficiency (no shared overflow), specialization (different models per task), and parallel execution of independent subtasks. Examples include conductor-based systems with planning, implementation, and review agents.

An isolated agent invoked by a parent agent to handle a subtask in its own dedicated context window. Subagents prevent context overflow in the main agent by running independently, and can execute in parallel for tasks that can be split into independent parts.

A security mechanism that restricts file system and network access for terminal commands executed by AI agents. Sandboxed commands have read/write access only to the current workspace, and network access can be limited to trusted domains. Helps mitigate risks from agent-executed commands.

Rich, interactive UI components rendered by MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers directly in the chat client. Enables models to display visualizations like flame graphs, flowcharts, and data dashboards inline, providing visual context alongside text-based responses.

Tokens generated by a model's internal reasoning process before producing a visible response. Thinking tokens consume context budget and are billed as output, but can dramatically improve quality on complex tasks. On current Claude models the amount of thinking is controlled with adaptive thinking and effort rather than a budget_tokens cap.

An open protocol that connects AI applications to external tools, data, and prompts through MCP servers. The current specification version is 2026-07-28, which makes the protocol stateless with a server/discover method; MCP was donated to the Agentic AI Foundation on 2025-12-09.

An open-format Markdown file at the repository root that tells coding agents how to work in a project: build and test commands, conventions, and gotchas. It works like a README written for agents instead of humans.

A Markdown memory file that Claude Code loads into context at the start of a session. It can live at the user level, at the project root, or in subdirectories, and holds the instructions and commands the agent should always know.

A repository file, .github/copilot-instructions.md, whose contents GitHub Copilot adds to chat requests in that repository. Path-specific variants live in .github/instructions/ as *.instructions.md files with an applyTo glob.

Instructions that apply only when the agent works on files matching a glob pattern, so context stays relevant to the code being edited. Cursor project rules use globs and descriptions to decide when each rule is attached.
A reusable Markdown prompt (*.prompt.md) in VS Code that runs as a slash command in chat. Its frontmatter can set the agent, model, and tools to use.

A VS Code chat persona defined in an .agent.md file (formerly called a chat mode) that bundles instructions, a tool list, and optionally a model. Custom agents are selected from the Agent dropdown in the Chat view rather than @-mentioned.
A Claude Code package that bundles commands, agents, skills, hooks, and MCP servers behind one manifest (.claude-plugin/plugin.json), installable from a plugin marketplace.

A Claude Code feature where the agent saves what it learns during a session, such as build commands or user preferences, to a per-project memory directory and loads it again in later sessions, without the user editing CLAUDE.md by hand.

A local JSONL log of every message and tool call in an agent session. Claude Code stores transcripts under ~/.claude/projects, one file per session, which usage trackers can read to measure real token consumption.
A server-side tool that lets the model search a large tool catalog on demand. Tools marked defer_loading: true are left out of the context window until the model finds and loads the ones it needs.
Claude calls your tools from inside code execution instead of making one model round trip per call, so intermediate results are processed in code and only the final output enters the context window.

A thinking mode (thinking: {type: "adaptive"}) where the model decides when and how much to reason, steered by effort. It replaces fixed budget_tokens thinking budgets, which return a 400 error on Claude Opus 4.7 and later and on 5.x models.

A rule on recent Claude models (Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5) that binds thinking blocks to the model and conversation that produced them, so editing earlier turns invalidates them. Agent harnesses should keep history append-only.
A system-role message appended to the messages array to add operator instructions partway through a conversation without editing the top-level system prompt, which keeps the cached prefix intact.

An advisory token budget for an agentic loop (output_config.task_budget, beta) that the model sees as a countdown, so it paces its work and finishes cleanly instead of being cut off. The minimum total is 20,000 tokens.
How long a cached prompt prefix stays available. On Claude the default TTL is 5 minutes, with writes at 1.25x base input; a 1-hour TTL is available with writes at 2x base input.

The smallest prompt prefix that can be cached; shorter prefixes are processed without caching. On Claude it is 512 tokens on most 5.x models, 1,024 on Opus 4.8, Sonnet 4.x, and Sonnet 5, 2,048 on Opus 4.7, and 4,096 on Opus 4.5, Opus 4.6, and Haiku 4.5.

Prompt caches match on prefix in the order tools, system, messages, so a change invalidates its own level and everything after it. Changing tool definitions invalidates the whole cache; changing a late message only affects what follows it.

A context management strategy that replaces old tool outputs with short placeholders instead of summarizing them with an LLM. On SWE-bench Verified it halved cost relative to the raw agent while matching the solve rate of LLM summarization.

Token counts for the same text change between tokenizer versions. The tokenizer introduced with Claude Opus 4.7 produces about 30% more tokens for the same text than earlier Claude tokenizers, so budgets and cost estimates need re-measuring after a model switch.

What a session's tokens would cost at API list prices. It is a yardstick for usage on subscription plans such as Claude Pro or Max, which are not billed per token, so it is not what the subscriber actually pays.
